info.name: iTunes / Apple Music — Music Discovery catalog provider
info.description:
Every upstream call the web player's catalog adapter makes.

The adapter lives at `frontend/src/server/providers/itunes.ts`; each request here maps to one method on the `MusicProvider` interface, and the folder descriptions say which.

**No authentication.** Apple's Search API is public and needs no key, which is the main reason it was chosen — see `frontend/README.md`.

**Two things worth knowing before you use this:**

1. The response `Content-Type` is `text/javascript`, not `application/json`. Postman still renders it as JSON, but a strict client that switches on content type will not.
2. There are **no CORS headers** on the metadata API, which is why the app proxies it through its own `/api/music/*` routes rather than calling it from the browser. The *audio* CDN does send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so playback works directly.

Requests are chained: run the Search folder first and the lookups pick up the ids automatically via collection variables.

item.name: 1. Search
item.description:
Backs `provider.search()`.

The adapter fires five of these **in parallel** rather than one `entity=all` call. Apple's combined search returns a single ranked list dominated by whichever type matched best, so the Albums tab would routinely come back empty on a query that mostly matched songs.

request.description:
Fields the adapter reads: `trackId`, `trackName`, `artistId`, `artistName`, `collectionId`, `trackTimeMillis`, `trackExplicitness`, `previewUrl`, `trackViewUrl`, `artworkUrl100`.

`previewUrl` is the **30-second clip** — the only audio Apple publishes. There is no full-length field.

`artistName` bakes collaborators into one string ("Atif Aslam & Pritam") while `artistId` identifies only the first, which is why the adapter splits the string and gives the rest synthetic `name:`-prefixed ids.

exec: // Chain into the batch lookup and the audio request below.

request.description:
Fields read: `collectionId`, `collectionName`, `collectionType`, `trackCount`, `releaseDate`, `copyright`, `primaryGenreName`, `artworkUrl100`.

The adapter derives album *kind* from the title suffix — Apple appends ` - Single` and ` - EP` — plus `collectionType` for compilations, because there is no explicit kind field.

`artworkUrl100` ends `/100x100bb.jpg`; swapping the dimensions in the path is the documented way to get a larger render. The app requests 600x600.

Fields read: `artistId`, `artistName`, `primaryGenreName`, `artistLinkUrl`.

**Artist results carry no artwork and no biography.** That is why the app's artist pages fall back to a deterministic Unsplash photo, and why 'monthly listeners' is derived from a hash of the id rather than read from a field — no free provider publishes that metric, and randomising it would make the number change between the server render and hydration.

// Documents the gap the app works around rather than asserting a success.

request.description:
Fields read: `collectionId`, `collectionName`, `artistName` (the publisher), `feedUrl`, `artworkUrl100`.

`feedUrl` matters most: **Apple returns shows but never their episodes**, so the RSS feed is the only source for those. See the 'Podcast RSS feed' request at the bottom.

request.description:
Search-result episodes have a real `trackId`, unlike feed-parsed ones which have no stable provider id and get a synthetic `<showId>-ep-<n>`.

Unlike music, an episode's `previewUrl`/`episodeUrl` is the **whole episode**, not a clip.

item.name: 2. Lookup
item.description:
Backs `provider.album()`, `albumTracks()`, `artist()`, `artistAlbums()`, `artistTopTracks()` and `tracks()`.

One endpoint, four shapes, distinguished by the `entity` parameter. The response always leads with the looked-up entity and follows with its children, already in disc/track order — the adapter filters on `wrapperType` to split them.

request.description:
`results[0]` is the collection (`wrapperType: "collection"`); the rest are its tracks (`wrapperType: "track"`) **already in running order**, so the adapter's filter preserves it for free.

This one call backs the whole album page — which is why `/api/music/album/:id` returns the album and its tracks in a single response rather than splitting them across two routes.

exec: pm.test('tracks come back in running order', function () {

request.description: Returns a single `wrapperType: "artist"` record — name, genre, and a link to their Apple Music page. Nothing else. No image, no bio, no follower or listener counts.
Backs the Discography section and `/artist/:id/discography/all`. The adapter sorts by `releaseDate` descending — Apple's own order is not chronological.

Backs the artist page's 'Popular' list.

Apple returns these in its own relevance order and publishes **no play counts**, so the app shows no plays column on this list — inventing one would be fabricating data.

Comma-separated ids. Backs `provider.tracks()`, which rehydrates anything that stored only ids — Liked Songs, a user playlist, a restored queue.

**Apple caps a lookup at 200 ids**, so the adapter chunks. It also re-sorts the response back into the order asked for, because Apple does not preserve it and the queue depends on it.
Backs `provider.show()`. Returns the show and its `feedUrl` — the episodes come from the feed, not from here.

item.name: 3. Charts
item.description:
Backs `provider.chart()` and the home page's 'Top songs today' shelf.

A different host and a different shape from the Search API — this is Apple's marketing RSS feed, not iTunes Search.

request.description:
**Lowercase country code** here, unlike the Search API which takes uppercase.

The old host `rss.applemarketingtools.com` returns a **301** to this one, so a client that does not follow redirects gets an empty body — that cost me a debugging cycle.

The feed carries ids and names but **no preview URLs**, so the adapter feeds the ids straight into the batch lookup above to get playable tracks.

// Chain: these ids are what the batch lookup resolves.

request.description: Same shape, but the ids are **collections**. A collection id looked up bare returns no track, so the adapter resolves each album's tracklist and takes its first track to build a playable list.

item.name: 4. Media
item.description: The two non-JSON requests. Neither goes through the app's proxy — both are fetched by the browser or the server directly.

request.description:
Run 'Search — songs' first to populate `preview_url`.

This is **why Apple was chosen**. The response carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, so an `<audio>` element can play *and seek* it straight from the browser — no proxy, no re-streaming. The metadata API has no such headers.

`Content-Type` is `audio/x-m4p` (AAC in an MP4 container). The `Range` header above demonstrates seek support; remove it to fetch the whole clip.

**It is 30 seconds. There is no full-length URL** — Apple does not publish one. Full playback of a mainstream catalog requires an authenticated paying subscriber and the provider's own SDK.

exec: pm.test('partial content — seeking is supported', function () {
pm.test('CORS allows direct browser playback', function () {

request.description:
Run 'Search — podcasts' first to populate `feed_url`.

The **only** source of episodes. Returns XML on an arbitrary third-party host with no CORS headers, which is why it is fetched and parsed server-side.

The adapter parses it with regular expressions rather than an XML library on purpose: podcast feeds are famously malformed, a strict parser throws on perfectly ordinary ones, and only six fields per item are needed. Each `<item>` gives the title, description, `pubDate`, `itunes:duration` and an `<enclosure url>` — that enclosure is the **full episode audio**, not a clip.

item.name: 5. App proxy routes
item.description:
The web player's own endpoints, which wrap everything above and return **normalized** shapes.

Compare these against the raw responses to see exactly what the adapter does: split artist credits into linkable refs, upgrade artwork to 600px, derive album kind, and drop provider-specific field names entirely.

Requires `npm run dev` in `frontend/`.

request.description: One response containing `tracks`, `albums`, `artists`, `shows` and `episodes` — the five parallel upstream calls, merged. Every search tab reads this same cached response, which is why switching tabs is instant.
`{ album, tracks }`. Note `album.artists` is an array of `{ id, name }` refs — Apple's single baked-together `artistName` string, split so each credit can be a link.
`{ artist, albums, topTracks }` — three upstream calls fetched in parallel and returned together, because the artist page renders all three above the fold.
Returns tracks **in the order asked for**, unlike the upstream lookup. The queue depends on that.

The home page's shelves, already resolved into cards. One chart call plus six curated searches, in parallel.

A failing shelf leaves a gap rather than taking the route down — with seven concurrent upstream calls, one flaky response would otherwise blank the whole home screen.
Chart ids already resolved into playable tracks with preview URLs — the step the raw feed leaves to you.

`{ show, episodes }` — the lookup plus the parsed RSS feed, in one response. Episode ids are synthetic (`<showId>-ep-<n>`) because RSS items carry no stable id; the episode page splits the show id back out of that to load itself.
